claims.text: Short-range chemical ordering or local compositional fluctuations, rather than constituent count alone, determine differences in deformation and failure behavior among CrMnFeCoNi and its FCC subsets.
Thermomechanically processed equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi can retain a single-phase FCC structure.
The equiatomic CrCoNi ternary subset can have a single-phase FCC structure.
All selected quaternary and ternary subsets remain single-phase FCC after the specified thermomechanical processing.
Applying identical thermomechanical processing will ensure comparable grain sizes and microstructures across the alloys.
Removing one or two elements from equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi can change its local-order signatures and mechanical response.
Controlling processing, grain size, temperature, and strain rate makes differences in mechanical properties attributable mainly to short-range order and local compositional fluctuations.
Local short-range chemical ordering or compositional clusters exist within the FCC solid solutions under comparison.
Short-range order or compositional clusters alter dislocation slip and faulting mechanisms during deformation.
Altered local element correlations modulate stacking-fault energy.
Altered local element correlations modulate dislocation interactions.
Changes in stacking-fault energy and dislocation interactions cause differences in yield strength, strain hardening, and ductility.
Relative to quinary CrMnFeCoNi, subsets with more pronounced short-range order or stronger clustering will have higher yield strength.
Relative to quinary CrMnFeCoNi, subsets with more pronounced short-range order or stronger clustering will have greater strain hardening.
Subsets with weaker local order will have lower strength than quinary CrMnFeCoNi.
Subsets with weaker local order will have lower ductility than quinary CrMnFeCoNi.
The proposed relationship is limited to equiatomic alloys in this elemental family that remain single-phase FCC under the specified processing and test conditions.
At elevated temperatures, transformations or other mechanisms may dominate the mechanical response.
Magnetic interactions or secondary-phase formation can interfere with isolation of the short-range-order effect.
A lack of correlation between measured ordering and mechanical behavior would falsify the proposed SRO-driven mechanism.
